opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and honestly it feels less like a pivot than a continuation. For a long time my work was about architectures, objectives, and pre-training: how you get the most out of a model per unit of compute. That was the main lever for a while. If you scaled pre-training well and got the recipe right, a lot of capabilities just showed up.

At some point, though, it felt like the frontier moved. Pre-training is still incredibly important, since it's the foundation everything sits on. But the most interesting gains lately come from what you do after it: teaching the model to think longer, to search, to check itself, to actually use the compute you give it at inference time. Reasoning and RL are where that happens. It's a different axis of scaling, and those moments are always the most fun to be part of.

There's also a personal side. I like being where things are still a bit messy and not fully understood. Architecture work matured a lot. We learned which tricks matter and which ones are mostly noise, and a lot of the "fancy" ideas got washed out by scale. RL for language models feels like pre-training did a few years ago. The recipes are still being figured out, the intuitions are still forming, and a small insight can still change what the model can do. That's very exciting for a researcher.

And I don't think the earlier work is wasted. Having a feel for how pre-training shapes the model, what the base model knows and what it can't do, makes you much better at the RL and reasoning side. A lot of what looks like "RL magic" is really drawing out what pre-training already put there. So to me it's all one story: build a strong base, then figure out how to make it actually think.

r001.rationale: The response says the frontier has moved beyond pre-training and identifies reasoning as a source of the most interesting recent gains.

r002.rationale: It discusses reasoning and RL as important post-training work, but does not say RL has become the main means of modeling in current practice.

r003.rationale: It calls the shift a continuation and says prior pre-training experience helps, but does not describe an easy transition or say Yi Tay had almost no prior RL background.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think it's less of a pivot than it looks from the outside. For a long time my mental model was that the architecture was the thing. You'd tweak the attention, the positional encoding, the scaling laws, and that's where the gains came from. And a lot of that work was real and I'm proud of it. But somewhere around the time pre-training started to feel like a solved recipe, at least in the sense that everyone converged on roughly the same transformer with roughly the same data mix, I started getting bored. Not bored in a dismissive way, bored in the sense that the marginal unit of insight per experiment was dropping.

What pulled me toward reasoning and RL is that the interesting variance moved. If you take two models with basically identical pre-training, the thing that separates them now is what you do after. How you elicit the behaviour, how you let the model use test-time compute, how you reward it, what the verifier looks like. That's where the leverage is. And it reminds me a lot of the early architecture days, actually, where nobody had the recipe yet and you could run an experiment on a Tuesday and learn something nobody else knew.

The other thing, and this is a bit more personal, is that pre-training is a very capital-intensive game. You need the compute, you need the data pipeline, you need a big team. RL and reasoning work is also expensive, don't get me wrong, but there's a lot more room for a good idea to beat a bigger cluster. The post-training stage is where cleverness still pays, and I like being in the part of the stack where cleverness still pays.

And then there's just the problem itself. Getting a model to actually think, to search, to backtrack, to know when it's wrong, that's a much deeper question than how many heads your attention layer has. I spent years making models bigger and faster. Now I'd like to make them smarter, and I think those are genuinely different problems.

r001.rationale: The response presents reasoning as a deeper, emerging research problem and says he wants to focus on making models smarter.

r002.rationale: It discusses RL as an important post-training approach, but does not say RL has become the main means of modeling in current practice.

r003.rationale: It does not describe his prior RL background or say the transition into RL research was relatively easy.

astra-6.text:
For me, the common thread is figuring out where the next big improvement in models is going to come from. With architectures and pre-training, you’re asking how to build a better foundation—how to get more capability out of the compute you spend. Reasoning and reinforcement learning open up another dimension: what can the model learn by trying something, getting feedback, and trying again?

What I find exciting is that you don’t necessarily have to specify every step of the behavior you want. If you can evaluate the outcome, you can give the model room to discover how to get there. That raises some really interesting research questions. Is it learning a strategy that generalizes? Is spending more time on a problem actually helping? How do you distinguish better reasoning from simply producing longer answers?

So I see it as a continuation of the same interest. You still need a strong foundation, but now you’re also asking how to turn that foundation into something that can work through harder problems.

r001.rationale: The response frames reasoning as an additional dimension for improving models and as part of the next stage of research.

r003.rationale: It does not describe Yi Tay’s transition into reinforcement learning research or mention his prior experience.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, there’s a natural connection. With architectures and pre-training, you’re asking how to build a model that learns effectively. With reasoning and reinforcement learning, you’re asking how to get that model to do more with what it has learned—to work through a problem, check an approach, and improve from feedback.

What draws me in is that the learning process becomes part of the research question. What should you reward? Which problems give a useful signal? How do you tell whether the model is learning something general rather than exploiting the reward? Those questions connect the training setup very directly to the behavior you want.

So I see it as a continuation of the same interest: finding better ways for models to learn, with the emphasis moving toward how they solve problems.
